text: Lesson twelve introduced governor limits as real-world rate limiting, and lesson thirteen named failure as the normal condition a system has to be designed around. This lesson goes deeper on the specific mechanisms that keep an overloaded system from collapsing: backpressure and rate limiting.

Backpressure is a system signaling upstream, based on its current condition, that it can't keep up and the sender should slow down — reactive, in real time. Rate limiting is a cap decided in advance and enforced regardless of whether the system happens to be busy right now. Governor limits from lesson twelve are rate limiting, not backpressure, because they apply the same way whether the platform is slammed or nearly idle.

If a fast producer keeps sending work to a slower consumer with no way to say "slow down," that work piles up somewhere, usually an ever-growing queue in memory. An unbounded queue eventually exhausts memory, and the process slows to a crawl or crashes — taking down requests that had nothing to do with the original overload. Backpressure is what stops that growth before it starts.

Two classic algorithms enforce a rate limit. Token bucket refills at a steady rate and lets requests spend tokens, so short bursts are fine as long as tokens have built up. Leaky bucket processes requests at a strictly constant rate no matter how fast they arrive, and overflow just gets dropped — no bursts allowed at all. The choice comes down to whether you want to allow bursts or smooth them out completely.

Even with a rate limit in place, a big enough spike can still push a system past what it can handle. Load shedding means deliberately rejecting some work rather than trying and failing to serve all of it — a fast "try again later" instead of a slow failure. A system that sheds load gracefully stays healthy for everyone else; one that doesn't risks serving everyone badly, or crashing and serving no one.

Backpressure reacts to real load, rate limiting enforces a fixed ceiling, and load shedding is the last-resort valve when both aren't enough. Next, lesson fifteen: observability, how a system tells you it's approaching this point at all.
